title: Opponents and neighbors
hookLine: Hasidism met fierce opposition from the Vilna Gaon's circle; today both ways of life thrive

cards: Every family has its big argument. How holidays work. What really matters.
Voices get raised, doors get slammed, and for a while it seems there's no way back. Hasidism had one too. It didn't spread without a fight.
Some leading rabbis of the time thought it was a dangerous mistake, and said so, loudly. Today: the opponents, and what happened to the argument.

teach.b: Mitnagdim means opponents, the ones who stood against.

Their leading figure was Rabbi Elijah of Vilna, called the Vilna Gaon, the genius of Vilna. He and his circle were alarmed by the new movement. The Hasidim changed the prayer book and prayed at their own times.
They put enormous weight on the rebbe. Some were accused of neglecting deep Talmud study for joy and song. For communities still shaken by the false messiahs of earlier generations, it looked risky.
The community of Vilna declared a ban against the Hasidim.
The conflict was bitter: bans on both sides, harsh words, even denunciations to the government. It's not a pretty chapter.
The tradition says Shneur Zalman once came to Vilna hoping to make peace, and the Gaon would not see him. But here's the rest of the story. The argument changed both sides.
The Gaon's student, Chaim of Volozhin, founded a great yeshiva, and his teaching stressed Torah study as the heart of Jewish life. Hasidism, for its part, held on to both its warmth and its learning.
Later, as modern times brought new challenges, the two camps often found themselves on the same side.
Today the Hasidic world and the yeshiva world, sometimes called Litvish, from Lithuania, both flourish, often on the same streets.
The Talmud tells of a heavenly voice that settled an old dispute between the schools of Hillel and Shammai: these and these are the words of the living God. Two paths.

how: Today Hasidic communities and the Lithuanian-style yeshiva world live side by side in places like Jerusalem, Bnei Brak and Brooklyn, each with its own customs, and study many of the same texts.

games.q: you're in Vilna. a new movement is changing prayer and putting great weight on its rebbes. the elders are alarmed. what did they do?
games.why: Vilna declared a ban. the fight was bitter, but over time both ways of life endured and still thrive.

practice: Think of a group whose way of doing things rubs you the wrong way: another team, another school, a rival, not an enemy. Ask one honest question: what do they protect that I might forget, what do they get right?
You don't have to agree; just find the one true thing in their way, and if you pray, pray for them.

wordCard.voice: Mitnagdim. The opponents of early Hasidism, led by the Vilna Gaon. The argument was bitter; today both ways of life thrive side by side.

orig.note: Hebrew: opponents, those who stand against. The name stuck to the Vilna Gaon's circle.

carryVoice: Your line: both paths endure. A bitter argument didn't get the last word. That's day three hundred twelve.
